content.text:
1. There are more than 20,000 known species of bees.
2. Bees live on every continent except Antarctica.
3. Bees evolved from wasp-like ancestors more than 100 million years ago.
4. Most bee species are solitary, not social.
5. Honey bees belong to the genus *Apis*.
6. The western honey bee is *Apis mellifera*.
7. A honey bee colony has one queen, thousands of workers and seasonal drones.
8. All worker bees are female.
9. Drones are male and have no stinger.
10. Drones develop from unfertilized eggs.
11. Queens and workers develop from fertilized eggs.
12. A larva fed royal jelly throughout its development becomes a queen.
13. Nurse bees secrete royal jelly from glands in their heads.
14. At peak season, a queen can lay up to about 2,000 eggs a day.
15. A queen mates on a few early flights and stores the sperm for years.
16. Queens can live for several years.
17. Summer worker bees live about five to six weeks.
18. Winter worker bees can live for several months.
19. Workers change jobs with age: cleaning, nursing, building, guarding, then foraging.
20. Honey bees use the "waggle dance" to tell others where food is.
21. The angle of the dance shows the food's direction relative to the sun.
22. How long the waggle run lasts shows the distance.
23. Bees have five eyes: two compound eyes and three simple ocelli.
24. Bees can see ultraviolet light.
25. Bees see red poorly.
26. Many flowers have ultraviolet patterns called nectar guides.
27. Bees can detect polarized light, which helps them navigate under clouds.
28. Bees use the sun as a compass and allow for its movement across the sky.
29. Honey bees beat their wings more than 200 times per second.
30. A bee's buzz comes mostly from its wingbeats.
31. Bees have four wings that hook together in flight with tiny hooks called hamuli.
32. Bumblebees can buzz-pollinate, shaking pollen loose by vibrating their flight muscles.
33. Tomatoes and blueberries benefit from buzz pollination.
34. Honey bees cannot buzz-pollinate.
35. Honey bees and bumblebees carry pollen in "pollen baskets" on their hind legs.
36. Many solitary bees carry pollen on dense hairs called scopae.
37. Bees' branched body hairs trap pollen.
38. Flying bees build up an electrostatic charge that helps pollen stick to them.
39. Bumblebees can sense the electric fields of flowers.
40. Bees taste with their antennae, mouthparts and feet.
41. Bees drink nectar through a straw-like tongue called a proboscis.
42. Honey is nectar that bees have processed with enzymes and dried.
43. The enzyme invertase splits sucrose into glucose and fructose.
44. Bees fan their wings to evaporate water from nectar.
45. Honey's low moisture and acidity keep it from spoiling.
46. One worker makes about 1/12 teaspoon of honey in her lifetime.
47. Workers secrete beeswax from glands on the underside of the abdomen.
48. Hexagonal comb cells store the most honey for the least wax.
49. Bees make propolis from plant resins and use it to seal gaps in the hive.
50. Propolis has antimicrobial properties.
51. Honey bees keep the brood area at about 34–35 °C (93–95 °F).
52. In winter, honey bees cluster and shiver their flight muscles to make heat.
53. Honey bees do not hibernate.
54. In temperate regions, bumblebee colonies last one year and only new queens survive the winter.
55. Bumblebees can fly in colder weather than many other bees.
56. A worker honey bee's stinger is barbed and usually stays stuck in mammal skin.
57. A worker honey bee usually dies after stinging a mammal.
58. Queen honey bees have smooth stingers and can sting more than once.
59. Bumblebees can sting multiple times.
60. Honey bee alarm pheromone smells like bananas (isoamyl acetate).
61. Stingless bees live in the tropics and also make honey.
62. Honey bee colonies reproduce by swarming.
63. In a swarm, the old queen leaves with about half the workers.
64. Scout bees choose a new nest site by reaching a group consensus.
65. Most solitary bees nest in the ground.
66. Leafcutter bees line their nests with pieces of leaf they cut themselves.
67. Mason bees build their nest partitions from mud.
68. Carpenter bees dig tunnels in wood.
69. Cuckoo bees lay their eggs in other bees' nests.
70. Sweat bees are drawn to the salt in human sweat.
71. Wallace's giant bee (*Megachile pluto*) is the largest known bee.
72. *Perdita minima* is under about 2 mm long, one of the smallest bees.
73. Honey bees are not native to the Americas; European colonists brought them.
74. California's almond orchards depend on rented honey bee hives.
75. For some crops, native bees pollinate better than honey bees.
76. The varroa mite is a major threat to honey bee colonies.
77. Colony collapse disorder was first widely reported around 2006.
78. The rusty patched bumblebee is listed as endangered in the United States.
79. In lab experiments, honey bees have learned to recognize human faces.
80. A rock painting in Spain, about 8,000 years old, shows a person collecting honey.
